opus-5.5.text:
I think we have to separate two questions. The first is whether the current architecture, basically the Transformer with full attention trained by next-token prediction and then RL, can *do* Long CoT. The second is whether it's the *right* architecture for where Long CoT is pointing, which in my view is autonomous learning and eventually online learning.

On the first question, the answer is clearly yes, at least for now. What we saw with o1 and R1-style models is that once you give the model room to think, with reflection, backtracking, and trying another path, reasoning ability scales with the length of the chain. The Transformer handles this reasonably well because attention can look back at everything it has written. In a sense the context window is working as a scratchpad, a kind of working memory.

But when I think more carefully, I see a structural mismatch. Long CoT is essentially the model learning *within* the episode. It explores, finds something doesn't work, and adjusts. That is a form of learning, but it's stored entirely in the context, in the KV cache, not in the weights. So you get two problems.

The first is cost and scaling. Attention cost grows with context length, and the KV cache grows linearly. If you want the model to think for a million tokens, or to work continuously for days on a task, the current setup becomes very expensive. Linear attention, state-space models, and hybrid designs try to address this, but compressing the history usually loses some of the precise recall that reasoning depends on. So far nobody has fully solved that trade-off.

The second problem is deeper. Context is not memory in the human sense. When a person spends a week on a hard problem, they don't keep every intermediate thought verbatim in working memory. They consolidate. What they learned gets absorbed, and they come back the next day as a slightly different person. Current models can't do that. When the episode ends, everything learned in the context disappears unless we run another training phase offline. That's why I say Long CoT is a first step toward autonomous learning, but the architecture doesn't yet support true online learning, where experience continuously updates the model itself.

So my judgment is that the current architecture is adequate for this stage. It got us from System 1 toward System 2. But it's probably not the final form. I expect future progress to require some mechanism that moves information from short-term context into long-term parameters, or at least into a more structured memory, while the model is running. That could look like test-time training, a memory module, or a new way of combining attention with a recurrent state. I don't think anyone knows the answer yet.

There's also a learning-signal issue that's easy to overlook. Today's RL for Long CoT relies heavily on verifiable rewards, like math answers or code that passes tests. For autonomous learning in an open environment, the model needs to generate its own signals: judging whether it's making progress, setting sub-goals, deciding what's worth remembering. That's partly an architecture question and partly an algorithm question, and I think it's one of the most important open problems.

In one sentence: the Transformer has carried us much further than many expected, and Long CoT shows it can support in-context learning over long horizons. But for real online learning, where a model keeps growing from its own experience, I believe we'll need meaningful architectural changes, especially in memory and in how learning gets consolidated.

r001.rationale: The response says current models cannot consolidate experience into their weights during use and that the architecture does not yet support true online learning. It frames Long CoT as a step toward autonomous learning, rather than full autonomous, continuous learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the answer has two layers, and they point in opposite directions.

The first layer is the one everyone talks about: context length, attention cost, the quadratic growth, memory for KV cache. Those are real engineering problems, but I don't consider them the fundamental issue. We've seen that with enough optimization, sparse attention, better infrastructure, you can push context to hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens. That's a resource problem, not a suitability problem. If it were only that, I'd say current architectures are fine.

The second layer is the one I actually worry about. When I say Long CoT is really a form of autonomous learning or online learning, what I mean is this: in a long reasoning process, the model is supposed to try something, observe that it didn't work, update its internal state, and try differently. That's learning. It's just learning that happens in the context window instead of in the weights. And here the Transformer has a very strange property. The "memory" of that learning lives entirely in the KV cache. It's a flat, append-only record. Nothing in the architecture compresses the experience into something structured. Every past token has the same status as every other past token, and the model has to re-attend over all of it to figure out what it already learned.

Compare that to what we'd want from a system that truly learns online. You'd want some notion of state that gets updated, where the mistake you made at step 200 changes how you behave at step 5000 without having to look back at step 200 every time. In gradient descent, that's what the weights do. In the context window, we don't have that mechanism. We're asking attention to do the job of an optimizer, and attention was never designed for that.

So my honest judgment is: current architectures are good enough to show that Long CoT works, which is already a big deal. The o1 and R1 results proved the paradigm is real. But I think they're not the final form. The models are doing in-context learning in a very inefficient way, and the inefficiency scales badly with how long the "learning episode" is.

What I find interesting is that this reframes the question. People ask "how long a context can we support," and I think the better question is "what should the model's state look like during reasoning." Is it a cache of tokens, or something closer to a set of parameters being updated? There's a lot of work now, test-time training, recurrent memory, state-space models, that's circling around this. None of it has clearly won yet. But I'd bet the architecture that's actually suited to Long CoT will have an explicit mechanism for turning experience into state, and the Transformer in its current form only gets that by accident.

One more thing. I think the training side matters as much as the architecture side. Even with a perfect architecture, if you train with RL on outcome rewards only, the model learns to produce the right answer, not to learn well along the way. So "suitability for Long CoT" isn't purely an architecture question. It's whether the whole system, architecture plus objective, is shaped around the idea that reasoning is learning. Right now it's mostly not. It's shaped around next-token prediction with RL bolted on, and the learning behavior we see is something that emerged rather than something we designed. That it emerged at all is remarkable. But I wouldn't call it suitable in the sense of being purpose-built.

r001.rationale: The response says current architectures can support Long CoT well enough to demonstrate that it works, while criticizing their efficiency and suitability as a final or purpose-built design. It does not judge that they cannot support it.

astra-6.text:
I would separate two questions: can the architecture support a long chain of thought, and can it turn that process into learning? Those are related, but they’re not quite the same.

During a long reasoning process, the model can propose an approach, examine the result, discover a mistake, and change direction. In that sense, the context acts as a temporary learning space. The model’s weights haven’t changed, but its subsequent behavior can change because of what it has just experienced. That’s the sense in which I would connect Long CoT with online learning.

Current architectures give us a way to do this, but I wouldn’t judge their suitability simply by how many tokens they can generate. The more important question is whether the model makes useful progress as computation increases. Can it recognize that an approach has failed? Can it preserve the useful intermediate results and discard the irrelevant ones? Does it have feedback that lets it distinguish a better solution from a more elaborate mistake?

Then there’s the question of persistence. If the model discovers something useful during one task, but has to rediscover it on the next task, that’s a limited form of learning. For stronger autonomous learning, we need some mechanism for retaining and reusing those discoveries, whether through memory or updates to the model.

So I see the current architecture as a starting point. Long CoT opens up room for learning within a task. The larger challenge is making that learning reliable, efficient, and transferable across tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says current architectures provide a way to do Long CoT and calls them a starting point, while describing limitations in reliability and transfer. It does not judge that they cannot support Long CoT as autonomous and online learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between a model spending more computation on a problem and a model actually learning from that computation. With Long CoT, the model can propose an approach, examine intermediate results, discover a mistake, and change direction. That gives it a kind of adaptation within the current context. But it doesn’t automatically mean that its parameters have changed or that it will retain the lesson for the next problem.

So I would judge an architecture by how well it supports that whole process. Can it preserve useful information over a long trajectory? Can it revise an earlier assumption instead of simply continuing from it? Can it use feedback to decide whether an approach is working? And can it do those things without the cost growing too quickly? A longer context window helps, but it isn’t sufficient by itself.

Current architectures provide a foundation for this because they can use their own intermediate work as input. The limitation is that much of what they learn during a task remains temporary. If we want autonomous learning in a stronger sense, we need a reliable way to turn that experience into something reusable—whether through memory, parameter updates, or a combination of the two.

For me, the important test is whether additional computation produces better decisions, and whether the system can carry useful lessons forward. Simply producing a longer chain of thought doesn’t establish either of those things.

r001.rationale: The response says current architectures provide a foundation for Long CoT and can adapt within a task, while noting that reusable learning is limited. It does not judge that they cannot support Long CoT as autonomous and online learning.
